title: Council Post: How Data Engineers Can Achieve Competitive Advantage
text:
By Jon Reilly, co-founder and COO at Akkio, working to level the playing field for AI in business.
Data engineers have an important job of transforming data into valuable insights for businesses.
Given the exponential growth of big data, and the ability of data engineers to manage and manipulate this data, data engineers are essential to a company’s success.
Challenges Of Data Engineering
That said, data engineering is far from easy.
The more data you have, the harder it is to make sense of it. After all, the average person can only focus on four pieces of information at a time. Even if we’re told that “data is the new oil,” more data also means more complexity.
One major obstacle is that the infrastructure needed to handle the data is costly and not available in most organizations.
This is particularly the case when building artificial intelligence (AI) models, which require a ton of computational power and specialized infrastructure. For instance, when building models for complex tasks like fraud detection, the size of the data required is huge. When you factor in the cost of renting hardware from cloud providers, model training and retraining and deployment, it can get very expensive.
Not only is it costly, but it's incredibly time-consuming, with 40% of companies taking longer than a month to deploy a single model into production. Engineers need to spend a lot of time just sifting through the data, building pipelines and doing other tedious tasks.
To make matters worse, data is often unorganized and siloed, which means that it's hard for teams to collaborate on analyzing the data.
Further, this level of complexity means that many less-technical people are at a loss when analyzing the data, and they can’t help but be overwhelmed by the sheer volume of information. As a result, AI remains out of the reach of many small businesses.
Indeed, while over 70% of medium-sized businesses use AI and machine learning, only 13% of very small businesses do. This gap indicates that traditional AI systems are still too complex for many businesses to use, which leaves them at a competitive disadvantage.
The Solution
No-code AI is one tool data engineers can use to make their work easier and enable businesses to achieve a competitive advantage.
These tools are easy to use and require little training. They also work on any data and can be deployed anywhere, which means data engineers can use them across industries and company sizes.
By automating the tedious aspects of data engineering, no-code AI lets teams quickly and easily build and deploy AI models, which in turn allows for greater agility and more time spent on innovation.
After all, AI is just a tool, not the end goal. With better tools, you can focus on what matters most: the insights and value you’re creating for your business and customers.
Real-World Examples
No-code AI is being used to achieve competitive advantages in many areas, from sales and marketing to finance and cybersecurity.
For instance, in the financial sector, no-code AI is being used to automatically scan transactions and detect signs of fraud. This, in turn, helps employees by freeing up their time to do other tasks — and it also helps these companies manage financial risks more efficiently.
Moreover, marketers are using no-code AI to better understand when customers are about to leave and turn to competitors. That way, these businesses can proactively engage with their customers before they walk out the door.
In the sales industry, no-code AI is used to find high-conversion customer leads, or even find customers who are disappointed in the solutions offered by your competitors, so you can then reach out to them with your offer.
Data engineers can help organize and source the data that fuels these models, helping businesses achieve competitive advantages.
The benefits of AI include increased productivity, decreased human error and lower costs. By automating repetitive tasks, data engineers can help businesses focus on actions that truly move the needle.
The world of AI is constantly evolving and companies are always looking for new ways to use it to benefit their business. Data engineers can use no-code AI to make businesses more competitive and achieve success.

title: Citywide Gunshot Detection Could Be Bolstered Via Roaming AI Self-Driving Cars
text:
Shots fired!
It is certainly startling when you hear a loud bang that sounds like a gunshot.
Imagine sitting in your living room and from outside comes that blaring sound. It seemed like gunfire, but you aren’t quite sure. There was a very loud noise, it was a sharp popping sound reminiscent of a gunshot, and it was close enough to be heard.
Luckily, the sound wasn’t so close that it might have been gunfire directed at or particularly nearby your home.
Should you call the police to notify them about the apparent gunfire?
That’s an interesting question.
Sometimes, people that think they might have heard a gunshot are reluctant to report that they heard the sound. One form of reluctance is due to their being unsure of what the sound really was. You don’t want to officially claim that there was a gunshot if the sound turns out to be fireworks, or maybe a car that backfired making an abrupt boom. No sense in wasting the time of the authorities to track down something that was relatively innocent and unnoteworthy.
Another form of reluctance is based on the belief that others will report the incident, therefore there is no need for you to do so. The irony here is that oftentimes nobody at all reports the gunfire because they all assume that certainly someone else is or has already done so. Police indicate that they will frequently find out after-the-fact that many people heard the noise and yet opted to not report it since they “naturally” assumed that someone else would.
According to some nationally reported statistics, supposedly only about 20% of overheard gunfire is being reported. One supposes that some don’t report gunshots if they believe that there is little valuable information that they can provide.
For example, people are unlikely to be able to definitively identify how far away the gunfire was. The glaring sound of a gunshot can carry for a lengthy distance. Perhaps the gunfire that you thought you heard is not anywhere close to your neighborhood.
Besides the distance away, there is also the matter of where or at least in what direction did the gunfire come from. Anyone that hears such a sound while quietly sitting in their home is bound to have trouble trying to provide a reliable indication of where the origin of the gunshot was. Maybe it came from somewhere far in the distance in front of your house, or perhaps it was more so toward the back of the domicile. Any shot that is far away will also likely echo around and it might be tough to pin down where it started.
Perhaps surprisingly, some people report gunfire and can even indicate that they can discern what type of gun was likely being used. These tend to be people that served in the military or that own a gun or otherwise have an interest in guns. For them, the instant they hear a gunshot, they can pretty much ascertain what type of weapon was used. Their ears are tuned to what gunshots sound like and how they differ by the type of gun involved.
You might be wondering why it would make any difference whether people opt to contact the authorities to report hearing a gunshot.
It makes a big difference in terms of protection for everyone and can demonstrably aid law enforcement efforts.
Somebody willing to shoot a gun while in a normal everyday neighborhood or community is endangering the lives of those that live there or that perchance happen to be there. We’ve all read the headlines about knuckleheads that fired a gun on July 4th as a celebratory act, and sadly the bullet or bullets came raining down and injured or killed someone. The shooter didn’t seem to be intending to produce such an outcome and got carried away at the moment, nonetheless, the act of wantonly shooting a gun is usually illegal and ill-advised.
Of course, the gunshot could also be associated with a heinous crime underway. Maybe a carjacking is taking place and the criminal has shot at the driver of a car. Perhaps a gang is having some form of a shootout. And so on.
Shots fired reporting by the public can significantly make a difference in many crucial ways. The police might otherwise not be aware of the criminal activity taking place. By being made aware, they can respond accordingly, possibly stopping the crime and preventing mayhem. Also, ambulances can be put on alert in case someone has been shot and medical assistance is urgently needed.
Okay, so it usually makes sense to report promptly when you hear a gunshot and provide as much detail as you can muster. When the police receive a multitude of such reports from the public, they can use the info to try and triangulate where the gunfire might have originated from. In addition, they can compare and contrast the reporting, using the bits and pieces of what people believe they heard to try and piece together a more robust picture of the likely particulars.
In other words, suppose a bunch of houses all have someone that opts to report a gunshot sound. If the preponderance of the reporting indicates that the gunfire came from the west, this is probably a telltale indication that indeed that’s the direction of origin. One house might say the sound was very close, and another might say it was faraway. By using those indications, it might be feasible to pin down a relatively specific location.
One facet that comes to play involves time.
People start to call about a gunshot after say a minute or two of hearing one. Some wait longer, some call sooner. Meanwhile, the clock is ticking. By the time that the calls are all reported, and the info assembled and analyzed, this means that the shooter has had an opportunity to scoot away or hide. Thus, the sooner that the reporting can occur and the faster that the analysis can occur, the more likelihood of being able to find and stop the gunfire activity.
This gunshot detection is a recurring problem in some cities.
To cope with the matter, there are technological capabilities that can aid in performing detecting gunshots. Here’s the way that it usually works (note that different forms of tech can be used, depending upon the circumstances at hand).
One approach consists of placing special devices at key spots around an area that gunshots are potentially expected to occur. These devices are typically acoustical, meaning that they listen for sounds and can measure the impulse sound waves produced by a gunshot.
In addition to listening for the gunshot, sometimes these devices will also use an optical sensor, seeking to detect the muzzle flash of the gun that produced the gunfire. You don’t usually think about the muzzle flash as a clue about a gun being fired. You might be surprised to know that the muzzle flash can create quite a bright light that can be seen from a large distance, especially for an optical sensor that is solely focused on detecting such a sudden burst of light.
Besides acoustical detection and possibly an optical detector, there is the possibility of using infrared sensors. Furthermore, some of the latest devices also include a video camera. The video camera is ostensibly used to either video the act of firing the gun or more likely is usually used to figure out license plates and the cars in a given area. The notion is that whoever might have fired the gun might attempt to escape the area in a car, and the video can provide a record of the cars that were in the area at the time of the gunshot.
The placement of these devices is a notable aspect of their utility.
Usually, the devices are mounted onto existing telephone poles, light poles, power poles, and similar structures. The device has to be high enough to be kept clear of obstructions and also not readily toyed with by someone that wants to bust the devices or muck with them. The devices are considered stationary and remain in their static position for however long their use is anticipated to be needed.
The devices also would include an electronic telecommunications capability. This allows the devices to immediately report when a notable sound has been detected (or muzzle flash, etc.). There might be software running on a processor of the device that analyzes the sounds and tries to determine the distance, direction, and whether it was a gunshot or something else that made the noise.
In short, these devices serve to report suspected gunfire. By having many of them, the reporting from the devices can be triangulated, similar to how the same effort is undertaken when people call to report gunfire. Of course, the beauty of the devices is that they are ready, willing, and able to report whatever they detect, doing so 24x7, and can do so with the kind of accuracy as feasible via the sensory units being used.
All told, the deployment of an array of these sensors can quicken the time of detection, which can then demonstrably improve the response time to a scene. This can also cut down on potentially wasted resources whereby the police and ambulances are sometimes sent to respond to the sound of a car that merely backfired, and for which the devices are unlikely to misreport that kind of noise as a gunshot.
The data collected by the devices can also possibly be used in criminal prosecution. When trying to tie the shooter to a scene involving gunfire, there might be few witnesses available. The devices can potentially provide needed evidence to showcase what took place and who was involved.
Not everyone necessarily welcomes these gunshot detection systems.
One concern is the potential privacy intrusions that might occur. Suppose the microphones of the devices pick-up the conversations of people that perchance are walking near the devices or live in the vicinity of them. Also, the video cameras are presumably going to capture the license plates of all vehicular traffic, and this might seem disturbing to those that live in the area. Etc.
Communities that seek to put up a gunshot detection system will oftentimes wrestle with the benefits of the capabilities versus the downsides of using such tech. There are ways to try and mitigate the privacy qualms, though there are tradeoffs involved. In any case, there is no denying the aspect that the gunshot detection system is likely going to do a good job of detecting gunfire, albeit with other caveats surrounding the use of such a system generally.
If a community wants to use a gunshot detection system, they will need to either purchase the devices or license their use. There is a cost involved. The devices need to be posted at the respective locations identified as suitable. There is a cost involved in posting them. Over time, assuming the devices are kept in place, there will be maintenance possibly needed, or units replaced if they get damaged by accident or on purpose. There is a cost for that too. Eventually, it is conceivable that the devices will no longer be needed, and there might be a cost involved in taking them down.
I bring up this point to merely indicate that there is no free lunch about using a gunshot detection system. There are various costs involved, naturally so. That being said, communities that are living under the specter of gunfire are likely to do a cost-benefit analysis and ascertain that the potential for saving lives and turning the community back toward one of safety is worth the cost.
Suppose there was another means to potentially detect gunfire, doing so in a manner that might not seem readily apparent.
Get ready and sit down for this one.
In the future, we will inevitably have self-driving cars (for my coverage see the link here). These are cars that are driven by an AI driving system. There isn’t a human at the wheel. The belief is that we will eventually have self-driving cars that are serving as ridesharing vehicles, proffering rides at a fraction of the cost of today’s human-driven ridesharing options.
One vision of the future is that there will be self-driving cars relatively commonly cruising around, waiting for someone that needs a lift to make a request. Unlike a human driver that might be roaming around and awaiting a ridesharing customer, the AI driving system can easily drive 24x7 and just keep going and going. There aren’t any rest breaks or food breaks needed.
Self-driving cars are loaded with state-of-the-art sensory devices. Those sensors are used to figure out the driving scene. Via sensors such as video cameras, radar, LIDAR, ultrasonic units, thermal imagining, and the like, the AI driving system collects the detected data and tries to mathematically calculate where to drive.
Here’s where I am going with this.
Imagine if we could leverage those self-driving cars to become a kind of gunshot detection system. This might be a handy means to rapidly identify when gunfire occurs. In that manner, you are getting two birds with one stone. The self-driving cars are already roaming for use as passenger transportation, and they could potentially do double duty as a gunshot detector.
Today’s intriguing question is this: Would it be feasible to leverage the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars in a quest to undertake the detection of potential gunfire?
Let’s unpack the matter and see.
Understanding The Levels Of Self-Driving Cars
As a clarification, true self-driving cars are ones that the AI drives the car entirely on its own and there isn’t any human assistance during the driving task.
These driverless vehicles are considered Level 4 and Level 5 (see my explanation at this link here), while a car that requires a human driver to co-share the driving effort is usually considered at Level 2 or Level 3. The cars that co-share the driving task are described as being semi-autonomous, and typically contain a variety of automated add-on’s that are referred to as ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems).
There is not yet a true self-driving car at Level 5, which we don’t yet even know if this will be possible to achieve, and nor how long it will take to get there.
Meanwhile, the Level 4 efforts are gradually trying to get some traction by undergoing very narrow and selective public roadway trials, though there is controversy over whether this testing should be allowed per se (we are all life-or-death guinea pigs in an experiment taking place on our highways and byways, some contend, see my coverage at this link here).
Since semi-autonomous cars require a human driver, the adoption of those types of cars won’t be markedly different than driving conventional vehicles, so there’s not much new per se to cover about them on this topic (though, as you’ll see in a moment, the points next made are generally applicable).
For semi-autonomous cars, it is important that the public needs to be forewarned about a disturbing aspect that’s been arising lately, namely that despite those human drivers that keep posting videos of themselves falling asleep at the wheel of a Level 2 or Level 3 car, we all need to avoid being misled into believing that the driver can take away their attention from the driving task while driving a semi-autonomous car.
You are the responsible party for the driving actions of the vehicle, regardless of how much automation might be tossed into a Level 2 or Level 3.
Self-Driving Cars And Gunshot Detection
For Level 4 and Level 5 true self-driving vehicles, there won’t be a human driver involved in the driving task.
All occupants will be passengers.
The AI is doing the driving.
One aspect about self-driving cars that I keep pressing on is the notion of what I refer to as the roving eye (see my analysis at this link here). Essentially, self-driving cars are going to capture on video and via their other sensors the everyday world around us. When a self-driving car goes down your block, it will video and collect data about the homes, the cars parked in driveways and on the streets, and even video that shows you and your kids are playing in your front yard.
This data is sometimes being immediately discarded by the on-board processors and only used from moment-to-moment for purposes of determining the driving aspects of the vehicle. In other cases, the data is collected into an internal database on-board the car. Furthermore, the data is at times uploaded via OTA (Over-The-Air) electronic communications into the cloud being used by the fleet operator or the automaker.
It would make sense to collect the data and make use of it. For example, the data could be utilized to potentially improve the driving capability of the AI driving system. I’ve also pointed out that the data could be used in a myriad of other very positive ways, such as providing ongoing and timely info about real estate in a given area, and so on.
The use of the data could also be used as a crime deterrent. If a criminal tries to commit a crime, there is a chance that a roaming self-driving car might have caught them on video. It could be that a multitude of roving self-driving cars each caught the crook in different stages of the crime, and the pieces of that puzzle could be put together to tell the whole story.
Could self-driving cars be used for detecting gunshots?
Yes, there is a possibility of doing so.
The sensors could be used to visually detect the gunfire and possibly detect the shooter. In terms of listening for the sound of gunfire, that’s something that would take a bit of an extra step. Allow me a moment to briefly explain.
Some self-driving cars do not yet have microphones on-board that are aimed outside of the vehicle. Gradually, this is happening, since the automakers and self-driving tech firms are realizing that hearing the sounds of an area can be handy for driving purposes (see my explanation at this link here). For example, the siren sound of a fire truck or an ambulance can be quite important when driving a car.
Whether the acoustical detection of the types of external-facing microphones being used would be sufficient for also reliably detecting gunshots is something that would depend upon how a maker has outfitted their self-driving cars.
Also, the software stack of the AI driving system is not going to natively have a gunshot detection capability. This is something that isn’t on the list of nearly anyone that is focusing on right now getting self-driving cars to safely drive from point A to point B. At best, the idea of developing a gunshot detection capacity is on an edge or corner case list, meaning it has very low priority at this time and might at some future point surface as something worthy of pursuing.
One of the toughest aspects of using self-driving cars for this purpose is the vagaries involved.
By vagaries, I mean that, unlike sensors that are bolted to a light pole or other fixture, the sensors of the self-driving car are integral to the vehicle and therefore are going to be in pretty much continual motion. They aren’t planted in a fixed position.
Furthermore, if self-driving cars aren’t perchance cruising around in your neighborhood when a gunshot occurs, they won’t be useful to the gunshot detection. This implies that the chances of self-driving cars serving as a useful tool in gunshot detection would be based on whether they frequent the area where gunshot detection is desired.
Some believe that we will ultimately have self-driving cars everywhere and at all times. In that case, we will be saturated with self-driving cars and they might perchance be in the right place at the right time to aid in detecting gunfire. That’s a long time from now, and so don’t hold your breath waiting for this to soon arise.
Nonetheless, it is an interesting consideration. We could potentially leverage the presumed ubiquitous nature of deploying self-driving cars and find another handy aid in doing gunshot detection.
There are plenty of added twists.
For example, there will be a multitude of brands of self-driving cars. This suggests that trying to get them to coordinate their gunshot detection would be logistically challenging. On the other hand, one supposes that they would each include a feature that reported directly to a central authority and left the analysis aspects to others. In that way of thinking, the self-driving cars are solely acting as data collectors and not doing the rest of the gun detection effort.
Conclusion
Some argue that it would make little sense for the automakers and fleet operators to enter into this gunshot detection realm. Those firms might be accused of serving a form of Big Brother that is doing the legwork for the authorities. Also, if their collected data was utilized for gunfire detection, it might end up being used in criminal cases and the automaker or fleet operator would get dragged into legal matters that seem quite afield of their emphasis on self-driving cars per se.
Another possibility would be for those specialized firms that are devoted to gunshot detection systems to pair with a self-driving car operation. In a sense, you could use the static sensors as one layer of detection, and leverage the self-driving cars as an additional layer of detection. It is easy to see that this might provide added coverage.
That last point is important because some might be thinking that the days of those that today provide gunshot detection systems are being counted down as the rise of self-driving cars looms ahead. Not so. There is a much greater likelihood of the two joinings together, rather than self-driving cars somehow driving them out of business (a bit of a rough pun there).
One final thought.
Recall that earlier it was mentioned that sometimes people do not report a gunshot because they assume that others will do so. It is conceivable, though a stretch, that if people are informed that self-driving cars are aiding the gunshot detection effort, people might be even less inclined to make a report. Their assumption would undoubtedly be that self-driving cars will figure things out and there’s no need for humans to do any reporting.
Anyway, the odds are that we are all going to discover ways to make use of self-driving cars in ways that are not yet apparent. Until self-driving cars are roaming our communities in a gaggle of sorts, we might not readily have insights about what they can be used for.
Well, other than the obvious use of giving us humans a lift.

title: Operationalizing AI Ethics, No Longer An Option But An Imperative
text:
A Virtual Sit Down with Reid Blackman.
As I’ve written in my “On AI Ethics,” series, machine learning models that aim to mirror and predict real-life as closely as possible are not without their challenges. Household name brands like Amazon, Apple, Facebook, Google have been accused of algorithmic bias that have negatively affected society at large.
While some organizations are investing in teams to ensure algorithmic accountability and ethics, Reid Blackman, CEO of Virtue and former professor of philosophy at Colgate University and the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill, says most are still falling short in ensuring their products perform ethically in the real world.
“Despite reputational, regulatory, and legal risks, it’s surprising how many companies that rely on AI/ML still lack the ability to identify, evaluate, and mitigate the associated ethical risks,” says Blackman. “Teams end up either overlooking risks, scrambling to solve issues as they come up, or crossing their fingers in the hope that the problem will resolve itself.”
When we built an end-to-end ML observability and model monitoring platform—an “on the ground” solution as Blackman calls it—our goal was to help clients address these issues by better surfacing, troubleshooting, and explaining anomalies in their models.
But solutions like ours are merely tools for an organization to wield. We agree, as Blackman suggests, that the answer to using data and developing AI products without falling into ethical pitfalls along the way, must involve implementing systems that identify ethical risks throughout the organization, from IT to HR to marketing to product and beyond. What’s more, as Blackman points out, “these tools can be great for those on the front lines of defense, but they also need the ability to elevate concerns to senior executives and relevant ethics experts.Engineers and data scientists often don’t receive institutional support and the skills, knowledge, and experience to systematically, exhaustively, and efficiently answer ethical questions are dispersed across the organization.”
There is no single right way to operationalize AI ethics given the varying values of companies across dozens of industries. Regardless of the approach a company takes, the best measure of its effectiveness is simple: does it make it more trustworthy?
Here are Blackman’s seven steps to operationalizing ethical AI, as outlined in HBR:
- Identify existing infrastructure that a data and AI ethics program can leverage
- Create a data and AI ethical risk framework that is tailored to your industry
- Change how you think about ethics by taking cues from the successes in health care
- Optimize guidance and tools for product managers
- Build organizational awareness
- Formally and informally incentivize employees to play a role in identifying AI ethical risks
- Monitor impacts and engage stakeholders
Today, machine learning and artificial intelligence systems, trained by data, have become so effective that many of the largest and most well-respected companies in the world use them almost exclusively to make mission-critical business decisions. For those of us working to ensure that these decisions don’t disproportionately harm underrepresented and disadvantaged communities, we’re far from alone in suggesting that ethics in AI should be center stage in the discussion. However, we’d be doing a disservice to the movement if we didn’t acknowledge that a siloed, technology-centric approach alone cannot make AI socially and ethically responsible.
Instead, we can agree with Blackman that an approach worth exploring is one that looks at ethics from an operational perspective, integrating the most appropriate ML infrastructure tools and processes where appropriate.

title: Is Artificial Intelligence Contributing Positively To Parenting? Weighing The Pros And Cons With Angela J. Kim
text:
With artificial intelligence becoming more and more a part of our everyday lives, it is important to consider how this evolving technology will affect the way we parent. It seems that most discussions about parenting and AI are focused on privacy issues, but there are many other ways in which these two worlds intersect.
Angela J. Kim is the creator of the popular lifestyle blog and podcast Mommy Diary, and the leading Asian-American voice on motherhood and lifestyle. Kim has worked with companies like Google, Microsoft and Amazon Alexa on their latest AI gadgets designed for families like Google family, Microsoft edge kids mode, and Alexa, and believes this will be a growing trend for families.
“What I learned in the early 2000s when I started Mommy Diary, was that in the parenting relationship, it is the parents that need help more. I started Mommy Diary after going through severe postpartum depression from my first two kids and it was meant to be a community that helped the moms get better, mentally fit, and stronger,” says Kim.
“I knew that this was the only way they could parent better. Artificial intelligence engineers should take a similar perspective; we need more tools that help the parents learn, grow, and stay aware than we need tech for the kids”
Angela’s point is one that has been echoed by AI experts as well. A few companies have also taken up the challenge. One such company created Muse, an AI-powered app that entered the parenting-aid space as tech-for-parents rather than the more popular, tech for kids.
Muse focuses on utilizing machine learning and big data to try and help parents raise creative, motivated, emotionally intelligent kids.
In the last few years, we have seen an explosion in AI-powered solutions purporting to help parents out. Chatterbaby, a smartphone AI app claims the ability to aid parents in understanding whether their child might be fussy, hungry, or in pain by analyzing the acoustic features of a baby’s cry, while Snoo, an AI-equipped bassinet coddles and calms a newborn freeing up the parent to rest. There is also Nanit, an AI Nanny that studies a baby’s sleep patterns and finds the reason for a baby’s restlessness at night.
However, resources that interface directly with the baby have been heavily criticized on different forums in spite of the obvious value they bring. Angela explains why this criticism is to be expected;
“Parenting is an emotion-based activity, a mom is naturally equipped with the intuition to know what her baby’s cries mean. We do not have many long-term studies on what it means to rely on this tech to interface with our kids. It is clear that they have some short-term value, but it is much safer to have AI tools that parents can utilize to better equip themselves with the art of parenting. This way our kids can enjoy direct emotional contact more frequently.”
Kim insists that AI has brought some value to parenting especially in the area of reducing stress for parents and moms. However, she does leave a warning; “A mother’s intuition is the best app for parenting her children. I advise that we use tools and not let them use us. Parents should accept every tool with a grain of salt.”
AI is not just helping parents with general parenting roles, it is helping our kids learn better. Google Read Along is a tool developed to help kids improve their reading skills fast. This is just one of the tools that are available to teach kids various skills.
However, AI cannot determine on its own when an external distraction is hampering their learning, or when a child is not naturally suited for a certain kind of skill. For AI to be more suited to be beneficial to parents, parents will still have to be heavily involved to guide it and to veto its decisions based on their intimate knowledge of their children.
There are a variety of AI tools that are helpful in improving children’s behavior and in monitoring their activities from TV-watch-time to internet-use- time. However, at the same time, we can not rely on them to teach our kids why certain activities are harmful or to train them on effective decision-making.
AI-powered cameras are available to help monitor your kids for safety purposes, but AI cannot protect them if something bad does happen. Parents have to use these tools to be better without relying on them to do the job of parenting.
One of the most groundbreaking innovations in the AI-for-parenting space came in 2020, when Avatarminds, a giant AI company released iPal, a robot that they claimed could take over about 50% of parenting roles.
iPal supposedly walks, talks, plays games, and dances as well as reads stories and plugs into social media and the internet. It also learns a child’s likes and dislikes incrementally. The bot can wake a child up in the morning and guide them through the morning rituals. The selling point is that it does this with “personality”, by leveraging its Emotional Management System to simulate human emotions.
Angela Kim, has spent a large chunk of her life advising mums on how to do the work of parenting and has built a multi-six-figure blog and podcast from this. She recognizes the struggles of parenting, but maintains a bit of skepticism with what she refers to as an “Impending over-reliance on AI and tech”;
“Moms are responsible for over 80% of household spendings, This makes them a highly valuable demographic. I recognized this great potential in the mom market early on and have since made tremendous strides in educating moms, especially special needs moms and Asian-American moms like myself.”
“Based on my experience, I think that pivoting to this impending over-reliance on AI and tech is risky. Special needs children for instance are not always deciphered early on and in many cases, AI robots could be useless to help them. Also, could a robot provide the authentic back-and-forth that helps children develop self-esteem, reciprocity, and empathy? Even if it can, will constant interfacing with tech not take away valuable time for real family bonding? Worse still, will it not take away the desire for it? We must answer these critical questions as we proceed”
However, Kim does believe that AI is a valuable tool for special needs families including iPads and kindles with digital therapy apps and various augmentative devices.
Additionally, Kim mentioned that she has used AI technologies like Nancy, Snoo, Owlet with her last child which wasn’t available with her older ones, and does believe they help parents facing sleep challenges during the first year.
The general consensus in the parenting communities is that AI should be used more by parents to better themselves and to perform tasks and less and less as companions for their kids.
This is not to say that AI tech should not be used at all, because parents need rest whenever they can get it. The proposition is that they should be overseen, regulated, and used sparingly to achieve specific goals.
“Task-based use” is what Angela advises, AI tools like Google Family Link, can help parents monitor online activity, regulate online purchases, and even shut down a child’s account if necessary. Net Nanny can help monitor social media usage.
There are also a plethora of AI apps and tools to help parents arrange their calendars and set up reminders for child-centered activities. These tasks are highly beneficial to parents and should be embraced.
A Task-based approach towards AI makes time for families to spend together as opposed to a “companion-based” approach which replaces parents with technology and in the long run, reduces the necessity for parents as mentors and advisers to their kids.
“A future with AI is inevitable, but it is not the answer to a growing desire to work more and spend less time with family,” says Kim.
“It should rather be the opposite, it should free us up from mundane tasks, help educate us and refresh us for the purpose of spending more quality time with family”
Angela’s words are instructive to both developers and parents moving forward. If the development of AI-solution becomes influenced by this school of thought, perhaps an AI-driven future would not look so bad for the family after all.

title: Tesla's 'neural net' is set to be the star of Elon Musk's AI day
text:
- Tesla's AI day comes just days after NHTSA launched a probe into its Autopilot system.
- The event will provide updates on Tesla's self-driving technology and serve as a recruitment opportunity.
- Here's what experts expect Elon Musk and other executives to discuss at the event on Thursday.
Tesla's AI day, set for Thursday evening at the automaker's Silicon Valley headquarters, could help set the record straight when it comes to Elon Musk's grand plans for self-driving.
Tesla's so-called neural net, which supports its Autopilot and Full Self Driving (FSD) technology, will likely be a primary focus of the event, Goldman Sachs analysts said in a note on Monday.
Musk is expected to provide updates on the company's AI progress, but any announcements are likely to face extra scrutiny following the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) announcement on Monday of an investigation into Tesla's Autopilot system and 11 collisions that happened under its control.
In the past, Musk has said the system, which comes standard with all Teslas and enables a car to steer, accelerate, and brake automatically within its lane, makes the car safer than competitors. However, experts have said the data released by Tesla to prove the point is misleading.
On Wednesday, two US senators further upped the ante, calling for the Federal Trade Commission to investigate Tesla's marketing practices around its Autopilot and Full Self-Driving software, dubbing it "potentially deceptive and unfair."
Thursday's event, scheduled for 5 pm PT, will take place nearly two years after Musk held Tesla's first "Autonomy Day," during which he made several lofty predictions about the future of self-driving cars. At the time, he said Tesla would have "one million robotaxis on the road" by the end of 2020. That didn't quite pan out.
The event will primarily serve to recruit top talent, Musk said, but will also provide insight into the company's progress toward fully autonomous cars. The event will feature a keynote speech from Musk, as well as several hardware and software demos led by Tesla engineers. Guests will also be able to test ride new vehicles, including the Model S Plaid.
Tesla's neural net is crucial to its self-driving systems
The system emulates the functions of the human brain inasmuch as it allows the vehicle to analyze its surroundings via cameras and determine what it needs to do when it encounters obstacles by identifying and labeling different routes and images.
The system becomes more accurate the more samples it receives, especially through real-world experiences rather than simulations, Musk says. To date, the neural network is processing data from Tesla's entire fleet — about 1.5 million vehicles.
Musk may also defend Tesla's AI approach that uses cameras instead of lidar sensors like other autonomous vehicles, most notably Waymo — a startup widely recognized as a front-runner in the race to self-driving cars.
The most recent beta version of Tesla's FSD software was pushed out as an update to select Tesla drivers in July 2021 through the company's early access program to the $10,000 or $199 per month software.
Goldman Sachs analysts also note Tesla is likely to discuss its progress towards its next edition of the software — an update that could help the FSD advance from a program that still requires a licensed operator to monitor the car's progress to a truly autonomous vehicle that does not require constant supervision.
Project Dojo
Tesla is also expected to discuss its progress on its super-computer, project Dojo. The computer helps label and train the neural network using the video data from the cars. Dojo is said to be one of the most powerful supercomputers in the world.
The carmaker hinted in its invitation that it will provide "an inside look at what's next for AI at Tesla beyond our vehicle fleet," which could include advancements toward solar storage and improved efficiency in manufacturing its vehicles, the analysts said.

title: City Leaders: Here’s Why Urban Tourism Could Skyrocket Due To AI Self-Driving Cars
text:
Urban tourism is oftentimes the crucial economic lifeblood that keeps cities humming.
Tourism-related employment is ranked in the top three of largest employers for approximately 60% of the states across America. When tourists make a visit to a particular city, the coffers get filled with those eagerly sought tourism dollars. This flowing money goes in every direction. Businesses do well. People get employed and are able to earn a paycheck. Funding toward city activities gets bolstered. And a veritable trickle-down of buckeroos makes its way throughout the urban setting, spreading delightfully like nourishing rain that springs forth vital economic and societal activity.
In theory, a city should do whatever it can to attract those tourism monies.
Some cities indeed are mindful of trying to allure tourists to their stately lands. They try to roll out the red carpet. Perhaps a city encourages the locals to be especially thoughtful and proactively helpful towards tourists. If you see someone that seems unsure of where the nearest touristy landmark is, gently and with civility point out how to get there. Provide insights about the best places to catch a bite to eat or to soak up the ambiance of the city.
Of course, not everyone necessarily welcomes tourists.
There is a decidedly love-hate relationship that can be had toward tourists. Yes, the tourists are visitors and admittedly adding to the financial bankrolls of the urban area. We should treat them as guests. But those presumed guests are sometimes quite annoying and there is only so much annoyance that someone can withstand. Having to deal with the wayward tourists that are clueless and boxing up the existing day-to-day living conditions is a bridge too far for some locals.
This can be readily seen in the roadways of a city.
You might realize that historically the emergence of the automobile in the early part of the twentieth century was a humongous boon to tourism throughout the United States. Whereas you normally think of “tourists” as visitors from another country, there is a demonstrative contingent of tourism that comes from fellow citizens that are seeking to be sightseers at cities other than their own. After a while, people tend to get bored with taking in the sights of their own city, so they drive to another one to get a fresh dose of excitement and experience the joys of being on holiday.
They are assuredly tourists in that context.
Anyway, the point is that the use of a car is instrumental to tourism.
There are those people that drive from another nearby city or perhaps from other outer areas and opt to become a tourist in the city of a chosen vacation destination. Some people drive from a faraway locale, such as driving from several states away and come to be a tourist in a seemingly far-flung city. One of the classic adventures for many families entails doing a lengthy family drive across the country and stopping at all the cities they’ve long relished being able to see while acting in a touristy capacity.
Besides driving a car to an urban locale, some tourists arrive via airplanes or sometimes via cruise ships. The odds are that some of those tourists will opt to rent a car for use during their stay. They become part of the city traffic as they dare to navigate their way around a city that is relatively unknown to them. Sure, they might have a GPS to aid in guiding their path, but this does not mean that the driving act is necessarily smooth and even.
Let’s be brutally honest, shall we?
Tourists of any kind that end up driving a car while in your great city are bound to foul up and make a mess of the traffic. These visitors might have the best of intentions. Nonetheless, once they are behind the wheel of a car, all heck breaks loose. They go much too slowly for prevailing traffic. They make crazy U-turns in the middle of busy streets. They turn without showing a blinker or they decide that they want to make a right turn while they are way over in the outskirts of the left lane.
On and on it goes, woefully so.
Locals that drive in a hustling and bustling city are readily able to carp all day long about those touristy drivers. Not only do those nutty drivers from out-of-town produce undue congestion, but there is also a solid chance that car crashes will go up too. The locals are caught off-guard by the wild antics of the tourist drivers. Bam, cars collide and people get hurt.
Some of the tourists probably didn’t want to drive to begin with. They would have preferred to walk around, but few cities are walkable in their entirety. The geographic distances are just too much and you cannot readily walk your way from one far-off tourist spot to another one. Furthermore, even if walking is feasible, there is a safety factor that comes to play too.
By safety, I’m referring to the notion that if you are ensconced inside a car, you are seemingly safer overall than if you are walking along on city streets. A person walking here and there is vulnerable to potential attack or other difficulties. Being inside a car is more than just a form of transportation. It is also a protective shield. You can get into your car as a sturdy bubble, plus you can quickly drive away from a situation that is becoming untoward.
This brings us to the usual counter viewpoint that the tourists ought to be using the mass transit options in a city for their traveling needs. Well, yes, that’s a good idea. Unfortunately, many transit infrastructures are set up in a manner that seems baffling to tourists. Seasoned locals might have the transit system figured out, doing so after many years of ridership. A tourist does not want to expend undue time and energy toward deciphering where the transit resources are, where they go, and how to make use of them.
That’s not what tourists usually hope to be doing on their days off. The gobbledygook of which stations to use or which benches to sit at are beyond their tolerance and touristy patience. By using a car, you can just get into the car and start driving. This might be less expedient perhaps than using the transit options, but it is easier overall and once again more protective and reassuring.
If you get lost while in the midst of a city transit system, you can feel totally out of whack and highly exposed. Getting lost while driving a car is not much of a problem. You merely turn around and head in another direction. Keep driving and you’ll eventually find your way. During those travails, you have air conditioning in case the outside weather is hot, you have heating in case the outside weather is cold, and can be listening to your favorite tunes.
A notable part of the driving equation for tourism includes the use of cabs and ridesharing (the latter is referred to as ride-hailing by some since today’s ridesharing is not especially about sharing rides and more so about hailing a ride).
Tourists have flocked to the use of ridesharing.
This makes abundant sense.
Take all of the earlier points about why people would prefer to be in a car, and you can see why using a ridesharing option is a strong allure. Even though the tourist is not doing the driving, they are still consuming the use of a car for tourism purposes. Of course, the trips are usually very short in duration, unlike if you had your own car or rented a car for an entire week of being a tourist.
In any case, a lot of the city traffic that is now taking place can be attributed to tourists that have decided to use ridesharing for their vacation travel needs. The cost though can add up pretty quickly. There is little doubt that in today’s city get-around options, using the transit system is certainly less expensive than using a ridesharing service.
Tourists need to weigh the tradeoffs of those choices.
Many choose ridesharing because they figure that the extra cost is worth the ease of getting directly from point A to point B. No need to change busses or switch from one subway train to another. You merely get into a car and it whisks you to where you need to go. You are willing to use up your hard-earned money to ensure that your time as a tourist is focused on enjoying a city and not consumed by having to dreadfully navigate the city.
The nice thing about using ridesharing too is that the tourist does not need to be at the wheel. There is a lot of stress associated with being in a strange city and driving a car. You don’t know the roads. You don’t know the local driving rules or customs. All of that is readily outsourced by using a local driver via a ridesharing service. The car arrives to pick you up, and a local driver is included. It’s a two-in-one package deal, even if just for that short trip from one touristy site to another.
A city that is known for having lousy transit or that has overly pricey ridesharing is often perceived by tourists as being less desirable than other cities that seem to have their act together. The mental calculus by a tourist about which city to visit is ostensibly determined to a great extent by what is there to be seen along with how much pain and suffering you will need to endure to get around that particular town.
Indubitably, you might go to a city on a one-time tryout basis and after experiencing the trauma of getting from place to place, you decide you’ll almost never go there again. Once was enough. On top of this, you might forewarn all your friends and colleagues to avoid that city like the plague, simply due to the high cost of intra-city travel and the byzantine and untenable ways to see what the town has to offer.
On the other hand, if you visit a city that was easy to get around, you might establish that it is now your favorite place to be a tourist. You are happy to go there repeatedly. The sights are worthy of seeing over and again. Plus, the local travel aspects are a breeze. This is something that you are glad to spread the word about.
How might a city then become more touristy traveling friendly?
The answer might seem shocking, so please prepare yourself.
Make use of AI-based true self-driving cars.
This brings up an interesting consideration in light of where cars are heading in the future. You see, the future of cars consists of AI-based true self-driving cars.
There isn’t a human driver involved in a true self-driving car. Keep in mind that true self-driving cars are driven via an AI driving system. There isn’t a need for a human driver at the wheel, and nor is there a provision for a human to drive the vehicle. For my extensive and ongoing coverage of Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) and especially self-driving cars, see the link here.
Here’s an intriguing question that is worth pondering: How might cities and city leaders leverage the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars as a tourist-aiming booster?
I’d like to first further clarify what is meant when I refer to true self-driving cars.
Understanding The Levels Of Self-Driving Cars
As a clarification, true self-driving cars are ones that the AI drives the car entirely on its own and there isn’t any human assistance during the driving task.
These driverless vehicles are considered Level 4 and Level 5 (see my explanation at this link here), while a car that requires a human driver to co-share the driving effort is usually considered at Level 2 or Level 3. The cars that co-share the driving task are described as being semi-autonomous, and typically contain a variety of automated add-on’s that are referred to as ADAS (Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems).
There is not yet a true self-driving car at Level 5, which we don’t yet even know if this will be possible to achieve, and nor how long it will take to get there.
Meanwhile, the Level 4 efforts are gradually trying to get some traction by undergoing very narrow and selective public roadway trials, though there is controversy over whether this testing should be allowed per se (we are all life-or-death guinea pigs in an experiment taking place on our highways and byways, some contend, see my coverage at this link here).
Since semi-autonomous cars require a human driver, the adoption of those types of cars won’t be markedly different than driving conventional vehicles, so there’s not much new per se to cover about them on this topic (though, as you’ll see in a moment, the points next made are generally applicable).
For semi-autonomous cars, it is important that the public needs to be forewarned about a disturbing aspect that’s been arising lately, namely that despite those human drivers that keep posting videos of themselves falling asleep at the wheel of a Level 2 or Level 3 car, we all need to avoid being misled into believing that the driver can take away their attention from the driving task while driving a semi-autonomous car.
You are the responsible party for the driving actions of the vehicle, regardless of how much automation might be tossed into a Level 2 or Level 3.
Self-Driving Cars And City Tourism
For Level 4 and Level 5 true self-driving vehicles, there won’t be a human driver involved in the driving task.
All occupants will be passengers.
The AI is doing the driving.
One aspect to immediately discuss entails the fact that the AI involved in today’s AI driving systems is not sentient. In other words, the AI is altogether a collective of computer-based programming and algorithms, and most assuredly not able to reason in the same manner that humans can.
Why is this added emphasis about the AI not being sentient?
Because I want to underscore that when discussing the role of the AI driving system, I am not ascribing human qualities to the AI. Please be aware that there is an ongoing and dangerous tendency these days to anthropomorphize AI. In essence, people are assigning human-like sentience to today’s AI, despite the undeniable and inarguable fact that no such AI exists as yet.
With that clarification, you can envision that the AI driving system won’t natively somehow “know” about the facets of driving. Driving and all that it entails will need to be programmed as part of the hardware and software of the self-driving car.
Let’s dive into the myriad of aspects that come to play on this topic.
First, you might be wondering why self-driving cars will make much of a difference to urban tourism.
That’s easy, the advent of AI-based true self-driving cars is anticipated to bring forth an era of mobility-for-all.
The belief is that self-driving cars will be available at a substantially lower price than a comparable human-driven ridesharing vehicle. This is primarily due to the excising of the human labor component involved in driving a car. The AI driving system will be doing all of the driving. As such, there is no need to provide rest breaks, no need to deal with driving fatigue or tiredness and otherwise be able to do away with the human-related driving woes.
You can add to the benefits that the AI driving system won’t be driving while drunk. It won’t drive while being drowsy. It won’t drive while being distracted from the roadway activity. All in all, a self-driving car will be able to run on a 24x7 basis and will not suffer from the usual limitations and maladies of a human driver.
In short, self-driving cars will be operated at a significantly lower cost than human-driven cars, will be more readily available and usable, and can be volume-wise scaled-up in a manner that trying to do so via hiring or contracting with human drivers is a lot less logistically onerous. This is why the mobility-for-all mantra is bandied around. People that today are mobility disadvantaged will now have an opportunity to make use of cars in ways that heretofore were prohibitive for them to do so.
Getting back to the tourist angle, the notion is that self-driving cars will be the go-to option for tourists.
Upon arriving at your fine city, a tourist will seek out the use of self-driving cars to travel throughout the town. The tourist would undoubtedly use a smartphone app, akin to how ridesharing services are requested today and select a self-driving car as their preferred driving option. This can occur on a ride-at-at-time basis. A self-driving car available on a ridesharing network would get assigned to come to pick up the rider, take them to their destination, and then the autonomous vehicle would continue doing the same with other requested riders.
In addition, it is also envisioned that a tourist might opt to reserve a self-driving car for their exclusive use during their visit.
The nice thing about reserving a self-driving car would be that the tourist can leave their stuff inside the self-driving car while they are on foot or otherwise outside of the self-driving car. When doing a series of disparate pickup requests, a tourist would not be able to leave behind in the autonomous vehicle their various knickknacks and personal gear. By reserving a self-driving car for a longer period, the vehicle becomes their handy-dandy constant companion platform during their touristy activities.
Another welcomed aspect would be that the self-driving car doesn’t necessarily need to find a place to park.
If you have a rented conventional human-driven car, you are continually trying to find a legal spot to park your rented vehicle. For tourists, this parking headache is a nightmare since they don’t want to get a parking ticket (nor be towed) and are unsure of what is proper when it comes to parking in the city, they are visiting.
As an aside, for cities that rely significantly on revenues from parking tickets and towing, you will need to eventually figure out how to cope with a notably reduced source of revenue. That’s why some cities are already discussing or putting in place so-called Zombie taxes associated with self-driving cars, see my discussion at this link here.
Self-driving cars are not usually going to be parked for any length of time and will instead be roaming around most of the time. Thus, the tourist can let the AI driving system figure out what is best to be done while the tourist is outside of the self-driving car, namely the AI will opt to drive the autonomous vehicle here and there or might find a parking spot to wait until the tourist becomes in need of a further lift again (the chore of parking is a task then for the AI, not for a human driver).
Okay, it seems pretty clear cut that self-driving cars are a big plus for tourists.
This in turn means that tourists might be more interested in visiting a city that has a lot of self-driving cars available for use. In other words, the benefits to the tourists will in turn attract tourists, which in turn will boost urban tourism for the city that has adopted the widespread use of self-driving cars.
There is also the novelty factor to be included as a bonus of sorts.
A city that has a lot of self-driving cars will possibly be able to promote the fact that the urban setting does indeed have self-driving cars. You could indubitably argue that the self-driving cars themselves will become part of the tourist attraction per se. People might flock to a city that has self-driving cars, partially due to the convenience of local travel, but also for the thrill and excitement of being able to ride in a self-driving car.
It is a twofer!
The combo deal is the ease of local travel that is then combined with the uniqueness and adventure of getting to ride around in self-driving cars.
That being said, over a lengthy period of time the adoption of self-driving cars is likely to eventually even out. A city that once was at the leading edge and was one of the few that had self-driving cars will inevitably become simply on par with other cities that have subsequently done likewise. The availability of self-driving cars will shift from being a novelty to otherwise being a standard expectation.
When that eventually occurs, which admittedly is a bit of time from now, cities that don’t have self-driving cars readily aplenty will find themselves at a potential disadvantage when luring tourism. People will be dismayed that the city lacks sufficient self-driving cars. Tourists will decide that they ought to use their vacation time elsewhere, rather than contend with the usual forms of more arduous vehicular options.
Conclusion
Could this all imply that self-driving cars are entirely upside and lack any downsides?
That would be an improper interpretation. As with any form of transportation, there are aspects about self-driving cars that might not be so welcomed in some cities and by some tourists.
For example, some tourists might say that they prefer the human-to-human direct interaction with a human driver. The local driver of a ridesharing service might proffer keen insights about the preferred places to dine or what areas to stay away from. All that localized knowledge about the city is seemingly no longer accessible if you choose to use a self-driving car.
Well, that’s not exactly the case.
The odds are that most self-driving cars will eventually have a slew of AI-based components onboard. This is bound to include a locally-focused knowledge base about the city and what to do in the city. Using an Alex or Siri type of interface, a passenger can pretty much get the same kind of insights about the urban setting as they would from a human driver. Indeed, some human drivers are huffy and difficult to chat with, while an AI-based chatbot would presumably be programmed to be either neutral or more favorably responsive.
If you really want that local human interaction, another possibility would be that while inside the self-driving car you could bring up the in-car LED display and make face-to-face contact with a remote human agent. Similar to using Zoom or the equivalent, the person could interact with you during your riding time. This is decidedly better overall than talking with a driver that you might inadvertently be distracting from the driving task itself.
All of that being said, some would still say they will miss having a human driver at the wheel.
This also brings up the qualms about how employment will be impacted in a city due to the advent of self-driving cars. There could be a lot of local city-dwelling human drivers that rely upon driving as a living that will now be displaced due to the use of self-driving cars. This could be bad news for a city, taking away a type of job or work effort that is nearly effortlessly undertaken by locals.
Though this is a serious concern, do keep in mind that it will play out over an extended period of time. The rollout of self-driving cars is going to be gradual, likely taking many decades. There will be a mixture of self-driving cars and human-driven cars on our public roadways for a very long time. We also don’t know how readily people such as tourists will take to using self-driving cars, whereas they might have a greater comfort level at using conventional human-driven cars. It might take several generations before enough people become comfortable with riding in driverless cars.
There is another factor that is related to the preceding topic, namely traffic and roadway congestion.
Self-driving cars are anticipated to be driven by AI driving systems in a rather strictly legal manner. They will not go over the speed limits. They will make a full and complete stop at Stop signs. And so on. This certainly seems sensible and you would assume appropriate to do (see my coverage at this link here).
The problem will be that human drivers aren’t going to like driving amongst these do-gooder driving systems and the cacophony of righteously divined self-driving cars. We’ve already seen that human drivers get frustrated by self-driving cars that won’t go faster than the speed limit or that won’t jackrabbit from a stopped position when a red light turns to green. See my analysis of these reactive and at times bullying human drivers at the link here.
All told, it could be that the traffic in a city will get even worse as a result of the self-driving cars being utilized. Human drivers will get exasperated and try crazier driving trickery. Meanwhile, self-driving cars might be endlessly roaming, rather than parking and getting off an active roadway, ergo they will be contributing to those massive tie-ups and overwhelming traffic clogs.
A key takeaway for city leaders is that they ought to be planning toward the advent of self-driving cars, encompassing the good aspects and the potential untoward aspects that might arise. And, for those that get there soonest, there is a potential windfall of attracting tourism due to the novelty of having self-driving cars and the ease of providing transportation for urban tourism purposes.
You might need a tune-up or possibly an entire overhaul of your urban tourism transit strategies, making sure to include those someday to be ubiquitous AI-based true self-driving cars. Don’t get caught behind the eight ball when it comes to ensuring that lucrative and synergistic tourism for your beloved city.

title: Cast AI Eyes A Hybrid Goldmine: Cloud Cost Reduction
text:
Debates about the true merits and cost of the public cloud have reached fever pitch among the cloud intelligentsia, some of whom claim that public cloud is simply too expensive at scale.
Identifying this as an opportunity, small startup Cast AI has identified one of the largest opportunities in cloud markets: Reduce the cost of public cloud by optimizing cloud compute.
First some background on the cloud debate, which has been raging on Twitter and elsewhere. In the cloud architect’s version of Republicans vs. Democrats, many technology experts are considering whether public cloud services are good, evil, or just overpriced. Central in the debate is the idea that organizations are starting to push back on the cost of public cloud services, which can rapidly escalate. Repatriation, in which an enterprise pulls back from public cloud to bring infrastructure back in-house, has shown promise in reducing costs and boosting profit margins. At the same time, there is more discussion about using combinations of private and public cloud services in hybrid setups.
Former cloud technology entrepreneur and Andreessen Horowitz partner Martin Casado has been on top of this discussion questioning the high costs of public cloud with lots of data – and pushing some companies toward repatriation.
“If you’re operating at scale, the cost of cloud can at least double your infrastructure bill,” says a recent blog recently penned by Casado and colleague Sarah Wang, titled, “The Cost of the Cloud, a Trillion Dollar Paradox.”
Casado and Wang have produced a nice body of work showing how public cloud can incur massive costs and hold down margins of some of the fastest-growing tech companies. As they recently wrote, “… it’s becoming evident that while cloud clearly delivers on its promise early on in a company’s journey, the pressure it puts on margins can start to outweigh the benefits, as a company scales and growth slows.”
In another Twitter thread that Casado has published as a blog, he asks whether there is a public “cloud margin crisis,” precipitated by the escalation of cloud costs.
A great amount of value could be unlocked by saving some of these costs. In a great example, Wang and Casado use the example of Dropbox: “When the company embarked on its infrastructure optimization initiative in 2016, they saved nearly $75M over two years by shifting the majority of their workloads from public cloud to ‘lower cost, custom-built infrastructure in co-location facilities’ directly leased and operated by Dropbox.’”
In their repatriation campaign, Dropbox boosted margins by 34% from 2016 to 2017.
Repatriation as a “Red Herring”
But is repatriation for everyone? Not every company has the resources and the tech expertise to pull a Dropbox. In fact, one of the main attractions of public cloud is that companies that don’t want to focus on technology can outsource much of it.
For such an entity, what if you could just lower the cost of public cloud? The tradeoffs of using public cloud for applications development are well known: It’s very convenient and scalable. But the costs can escalate rapidly – you are paying for convenience — and you can get locked in to one provider. If you remove both those “cons,” can public cloud be a no brainer?
This is where Cast AI thinks it has the right approach: Optimize your public cloud spend and make repatriation a moot point.
Cast AI was founded by Yuri Frayman (CEO), Leon Kuperman (CTO), and Laurent Gil (Chief Product Officer). The company raised $7.7 million in seed funding in November 2020, but if it continues to execute it’s likely to get much hotter with much larger rounds to come. Initial investors included TA Ventures, DNX, Florida Funder, and unnamed angels. The company has about 30 employees with plans to double by the end of this year.
The premise behind Cast AI is there is huge potential to reduce public cloud costs by using tools that can analyze cloud spending and suggest ways to optimize the cost, including finding cutting-edge cloud processing instances that may be offered below market rates. The key is being able to switch between clouds in hybrid mode to find efficiencies.
Cast AI software currently delivers the following:
· The software gives the customer to get a high-level overview of savings potential as well as a granular look into how much can be saved in each part of the infrastructure.
· Provides a breakdown of spot cloud instance suitability and where obvious savings can be found.
· Indicates instance types and quantities that are optimal for certain workloads. Gives suggestions on what are the optimal replacements in specific situations.
CTO Leon Kuperman says the main driver of cloud costs is fat margins for the cloud providers, who believe they have the leverage (mostly through lock-in) to charge as much as they want. One of the vexing realities of public cloud is egress fees, in which cloud providers charge you to take data out of their cloud. This produces the roach motel effect – you can check your data into the cloud but you can’t check it out. Kuperman estimates that some major cloud providers charge data transfer fees at markup of 30X or more.
“We have a basic oligopoly, says Kuperman. “Three main players are making cloud environments that are highly incompatible. Control planes are different, the way you do networking is different. The underlying commodities are the same, but the ways the customers use those commodities are totally different. That leads to vendor lock-in.”
Kuperman believes that the debate about repatriation – or bringing back services from public cloud to the private data center – is a “red herring,” because people really don’t want to do that. They like the convenience and simplicity of buying as-a-service. The only thing that may prove downside is cost and lock-in. Kuperman says if you can lower the cost and mitigate lock-in, people will be less inclined toward repatriation.
This could become even more powerful if cloud applications could more efficiently switch among clouds. For example, what if customers run their software in a private data center and “burst” to the cloud for more firepower when needed, also reducing the need for large capital expenditure.
Kubernetes is King
Cast AI is providing tools for cloud optimization, DevOps optimization, and disaster recovery, but it has other products in the works. A major focus is on suppliers of cloud Kubernetes services, including Amazon EKS, Google GKS, Kubernetes Operation (Kops), and Microsoft’s Azure Kubernetes Services (AKS). The CAST AI engine does this by using Cloud Service Provider (CSP) accounts to create the required cloud resources and set up multi-cloud Kubernetes clusters.
“We have focused on customers that are in the process of adopting cloud native,” founder Kuperman told me in a recent interview. “It's incredible to create an environment of portability. We like Kubernetes as the underlying [technology].”
Kubernetes, a cloud compute technology invented by Google, has become the de facto standard for operating cloud computing processes in the cloud. Kubernetes came on the scene as a management platform for applications using containers, a cloud technology that virtualizes operating systems (OSs), stripping out some of the overhead that is typically associated with running virtual machines (VMs).
But Kubernetes is also still relatively young and lacks many management tools. This makes the technology particularly suited toward public clouds, which can provide their own tools and scale massive amounts of compute instances. To make things more complicated, each cloud provider has its own Kubernetes “as a service” (KaaS? Sorry) – which operate differently.
This paves the way for what Cast AI sees as a huge opportunity – providing tools that make it easier for customers to evaluate costs of cloud services such as Kubernetes and choose which services are best at any time – automatically.
“The waste is rampant in Kubernetes,” says Kuperman.
Demos Shows Immediate Savings
In a demo set up for me by Cast AI, the software ran through a specific cloud operation and demonstrated immediate savings of 40% or more. In one situation, it found availability of a powerful AWS instance at a steep discount.
Of course, the specific situations will vary. But Cast AI and Kuperman’s views sync with the thread followed by Casado’s crew – that there is a lot of juice to squeeze from the lemon. If companies worldwide are overspending on cloud, the potential for savings is gigantic. And the total addressable market for cloud optimization could indeed be a trillion-dollar opportunity.
What about the competition? Indeed, companies other than Cast AI are focused on cloud cost optimization. Flexera, the publisher of the well-known “State of the Cloud” report, offers a platform to monitor cloud usage and costs. Flexera was acquired in 2020 by private equity firm Thoma Bravo for $2.85 billion. But while Flexera analyzes cloud spend, it doesn’t offer many tools for actively managing the spend by automating hybrid compute.
Platform9 is probably a better comparison to Cast AI, because it has a focus on running Kubernetes across multiple clouds. Platform9 often targets repatriation, rather than switching among public clouds. It’s more suited to large organizations such as service providers that have their own infrastructure.
Cloudify is another company that comes up in the search. It does focus on distributing Kubernetes operations across multiple clouds and targets “multi-cloud orchestration.”
Casado and Wang refer to Thomas Dullien, former Google engineer who has cofounded cloud optimization company Optimyze, which focuses on analyzing the optimization of code and how it consumes cloud resources.
Overall, it seems like this is a promising area for startups to target. It also seems like it’s early days in the “repatriate or not” process. At Futuriom, we’ll be digging into this in more depth. I’m excited to learn more about the process and the technology available.
